symptoms: Large, irregular greenish-gray water-soaked lesions on leaves and stems that rapidly turn brown and papery. White fungal growth appears on leaf undersides in humid conditions. Fruits develop dark, firm, greasy-looking lesions.
spread_mechanism: Wind-borne sporangia and splashing rain; thrives in cool, wet conditions (temperatures between 15-22°C and relative humidity above 90%).
treatment_options: Apply preventive copper-based fungicides or mancozeb before disease onset. Remove and destroy all infected foliage immediately. Improve canopy airflow by pruning and stake plants. Avoid overhead irrigation.
safety_notes: Tomatoes showing minor late blight foliage symptoms bear fruit that is technically non-toxic if undamaged, but diseased fruit tissue rots rapidly, tastes bitter, and often harbors secondary bacterial rot. Discard visibly affected fruit; healthy-looking fruit from affected plants is safe after thorough washing.

symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with characteristic concentric rings creating a 'target board' pattern, typically starting on older lower leaves. Leaves yellow and drop prematurely.
spread_mechanism: Survives in crop debris and soil; spread by rain splash, wind, and equipment under warm, humid weather (24-29°C).
treatment_options: Rotate crops on a 3-year cycle. Apply chlorothalonil or copper fungicides at first sign. Mulch around plant base to prevent soil splash onto lower leaves.
safety_notes: Early blight is a plant pathogen and does not infect humans. Fruits with minor surface lesions can have the blemish excised and the remainder consumed safely.

symptoms: Dark brown to purplish-black water-soaked lesions on foliage. White downy sporulation on the underside of leaves during morning dew. Tubers develop dry, granular brown rot penetrating into the flesh.
spread_mechanism: Cull piles, infected seed tubers, and windborne spores traveling miles in moist cloudy weather.
treatment_options: Use certified disease-free seed tubers. Apply systemic fungicides (metalaxyl/mefenoxam or cyazofamid). Kill potato vines 2 weeks prior to harvest to prevent tuber infection.
safety_notes: Do not consume potato tubers affected by late blight dry rot or secondary soft rots. The pathogen produces toxins and makes tubers unpalatable and susceptible to bacterial toxins.

symptoms: Olive-green, velvety spots on leaves that turn brown and corky. Fruit lesions become dark, scabby, cracked, and distorted as the fruit grows.
spread_mechanism: Overwinters in fallen leaves on the orchard floor; ascospores discharge during spring rains when temperatures range from 16-24°C.
treatment_options: Shred or clear fallen leaf litter in autumn. Apply captan, mancozeb, or sulfur sprays starting at green tip stage through petal fall.
safety_notes: Scabby apples are completely safe to eat. The scab fungus produces no human mycotoxins. The fruit skin can be peeled or cut away for aesthetic preference.

symptoms: Frogeye leaf spots with purple margins and light brown centers. Fruit develops a firm brown rot with alternating dark and light concentric rings, eventually shriveling into black mummies.
spread_mechanism: Overwinters in mummified fruit, dead wood, and bark cankers; conidia splash during rainfall.
treatment_options: Prune out dead wood and remove mummified fruit from trees during winter dormancy. Apply thiophanate-methyl or captan fungicide.
safety_notes: Mummified or rotting fruit should not be consumed due to unpleasant flavor and risk of opportunistic mold toxins. Clean parts of lightly affected fruit may be used if well trimmed.

symptoms: Small reddish-brown circular spots on leaves. Infected berries turn light brown, soften, and rapidly shrivel into hard, black, wrinkled mummies studded with pycnidia.
spread_mechanism: Ascospores and pycnidiospores ejected during warm rainy periods (21-27°C).
treatment_options: Apply myclobutanil or mancozeb fungicides from early shoot growth through 4 weeks post-bloom. Prune canopy for sunlight penetration and airflow.
safety_notes: Black rot shriveled grapes are dried and inedible. Berries unaffected on the same cluster remain safe to harvest and consume.

symptoms: Vibrant uniform green foliage, sturdy stems, and smooth fruit surface without lesions, spots, or abnormal curling.
treatment_options: Maintain consistent drip irrigation, balanced nitrogen/potassium fertilization, and regular preventative scouting.
safety_notes: Crop is healthy and fully safe for human and animal consumption.

symptoms: Broad, green, healthy foliage without chlorosis, necroses, or curled leaf margins.
treatment_options: Continue standard hill mounding, balanced irrigation, and pest monitoring.
safety_notes: Tubers from healthy plants are completely safe to consume.
